title: France Just Invited India to Every Session of the G7. No Guest Country Has Ever Got That Before.
excerpt: Modi will sit in on all six working sessions at Évian next week — a diplomatic first that says as much about France's ambitions as India's rise.
body:
France has invited India to participate in all six sessions of next week's G7 summit — a first that underscores how dramatically the relationship between Paris and New Delhi has evolved.

The invitation, confirmed by French diplomatic sources on Thursday, goes beyond the standard guest slot that India has occupied at past G7 meetings. At the 52nd summit in Évian-les-Bains, scheduled for June 15-17, Prime Minister Narendra Modi will sit in on every working session, from economic growth and trade imbalances to AI governance and the Middle East. France has described India as a "top priority" partner.

This will be India's 13th participation at a G7 summit and Modi's seventh consecutive appearance — but the first time it has been included in the full programme rather than select outreach sessions. For a country that is not a G7 member, the distinction matters.

**Why France is doing this**

The simple answer is strategic weight. India is the world's fifth-largest economy, the fastest-growing major economy (7.8 per cent in the March quarter), and a $315 billion IT sector that every G7 nation wants access to. But France's invitation is also personal.

Modi and President Emmanuel Macron elevated the India-France relationship to a "special global strategic partnership" earlier this year — a designation that puts France alongside only Japan and the United States in India's diplomatic hierarchy. The partnership spans defence (India operates 36 Rafale jets and is negotiating a second batch), civil nuclear energy (where cooperation continues despite the Iran war's disruption to global supply chains), and a growing technology corridor.

Modi will visit Nice on June 14 for a bilateral meeting with Macron before heading to Évian. After the summit, he will stop in Paris on June 18 for VivaTech, Europe's largest technology and startup event, where India is being positioned as a global hub for digital transformation.

**The Trump meeting looms largest**

For all the French hospitality, the most consequential meeting at Évian may be between Modi and Trump. Reuters reported this week that the two leaders are likely to hold bilateral talks on the summit's sidelines — their first face-to-face encounter since February 2025 in Washington.

The agenda is long and difficult. Trade negotiations are moving towards a first-tranche bilateral agreement that could close by mid-July, but Washington has proposed an additional 12.5 per cent tariff on Indian imports over alleged forced labour — which India has flatly rejected. H-1B visa policy, which affects hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals, remains contentious. A federal judge blocked Trump's proposed $100,000 H-1B fee this week, but the administration is expected to appeal.

Then there are the dead sailors. India has summoned the US chargé d'affaires twice in three days after American strikes killed three Indian seafarers on a Palau-flagged tanker off Oman. Opposition parties are pressing Modi to raise the issue directly with Trump. The deaths have made what was already a strained relationship — complicated by US tariffs, the India-Pakistan conflict, and Trump's repeated claims of having mediated it — even more fraught.

**Slovakia and the EU dimension**

Between Nice and Évian, Modi will visit Slovakia from June 14-16 for talks with Prime Minister Robert Fico. The visit is partly about Slovakia's EU presidency rotation and partly about manufacturing. Slovakia has courted Indian investment in automotive and electronics supply chains, and India sees Central European partnerships as a way to deepen its integration with the EU single market.

The Ministry of External Affairs has framed the entire trip as a signal of India's commitment to its broader strategic partnership with the European Union — a relationship that has gained urgency as both sides navigate the fallout from the Iran war, AI regulation, and the scramble for supply chain resilience.

**What it means for the diaspora**

For the estimated 1.1 million people of Indian origin living across Europe, the trip carries practical significance. India-France defence and tech cooperation creates jobs in both countries. The VivaTech appearance could catalyse partnerships between Indian and European startups. The G7 discussions on AI governance will shape rules that affect Indian tech workers from Bangalore to Berlin.

Moreover, this unprecedented invitation to all G7 sessions signals a shift in how the global community views India's role on the world stage, which can enhance political representation for the Indian diaspora. As India strengthens its ties with major economies, NRIs may find increased opportunities for investment and collaboration in sectors like technology and manufacturing, potentially leading to greater remittances back home. 

The trip's real weight is diplomatic. India being invited to all six G7 sessions is France's way of saying that the old distinction between G7 members and guests no longer captures reality. Whether the other six members agree is another question.
